Base directory for this skill: /home/agus/workspace/asermax/claude-plugins/mahou/skills/canvas

Load mahou:basics first. Then read `.mahou/canvas.md` if present.

# Canvas

## Documents

A canvas is one document, `<name>.tldr.json`, in a folder a loading skill names along with the name. When the user types the skill, the folder is `canvas/` in the change's scratch folder and the document is named after what it draws. A folder can hold several documents.

- `<name>.tldr.json` is the document. The server holds it while the canvas runs and saves every edit to it, from any tab. Its `canvasVersion` names its format.
- `<name>.svg` is its export, next to it.
- `mockups/` holds the mockups every document in the folder can draw, one `<kind>.tsx` file each. A mockup is the content of the canvas's custom `mock` shape, for anything the stock tldraw shapes do not draw, such as a screen. Its file exports `mockup`, a `MockDefinition<Props>` from `@canvas/MockShape`: its natural width, its default props and a function that renders them. The canvas draws a mockup with no natural width, such as the built-in `area`, at the shape's own size instead of scaling it, so its border and label keep their size however large the shape is. A `mock` shape's `data` is merged over the defaults, so a shape passes only what differs, such as `{ kind: 'login', data: { state: 'error' } }`. A `mock` shape draws its kind at the natural width and scales the drawing to the shape's size, so one mockup renders at any shape size. Adding, changing or removing a file in `mockups/` redraws the shapes in every open tab without reloading the page.

## Running it

`scripts/canvas.sh` runs the app over one document. Pass it the document's path:

- `start` installs the app on first run, starts a detached server for the document on the first free port from 5190 and prints the URL to give the user. A document that already has a server gets its URL back. Each document has its own server, so several canvases run at once, in one project or in several; `CANVAS_PORT` picks the port instead. It refuses a document saved in an older format and names the `migrate` command.
- `watch` prints one line per event: `click` for each "Send to Claude" click, and `voice: <message>` for each voice message, with the shapes selected when it was sent.
- `export` writes `<name>.svg`.
- `texts` prints every canvas text and arrow label, one per line.
- `migrate` brings an older document to the current format, keeping the original as `<name>.tldr.json.bak`. Run it with the server stopped. When it warns that a mockup received a variant string, rewrite that mockup to read its props from `data`.
- `stop` stops the document's own server and leaves every other canvas running.

Edits to the app under `scripts/app/` reach the running canvas only after a restart, because `start` copies the app into the cache. Run `stop` and then `start`, and reload the open tabs.

Build and edit the canvas from scripts run with `agent-browser` in your own tab, opened once on `<URL>?user=Claude` and kept open, so the user sees your cursor under that name. Every tab edits the same document live: your changes appear in the user's tab as you make them, and theirs in yours. The page exposes `window.editor`, `window.tldraw` with `createShapeId` and `toRichText`, and `window.canvas` with `notes()`, `step(at, change, pause?)` and the drawing helpers below.

Draw in steps the user can follow. A script's changes reach the other tabs together, so a script that draws everything at once shows the user only the finished result. Run each element as an awaited `canvas.step`: it moves your cursor to `at` (a shape id or a page point, or `null` to stay), applies `change`, and waits `pause` milliseconds, 500 by default. One step per shape, arrow or move, in the order a person would draw them: follow the flow the drawing explains, and join each element to what it connects to as soon as both are on the canvas, so the drawing grows as one connected piece and never as all the boxes first and all the arrows last.

- An area goes first, before what it holds.
- After the first element, each new element is followed right away by the arrow that joins it to what is already drawn, then by that arrow's label if it has one.
- A note goes right after the element it describes, and its arrow right after the note.

Draw a large batch in one script instead, without `canvas.step`, when a change creates or redraws many shapes at once, such as every tree rebuilt from a revised record. Stepping through hundreds of shapes makes the user wait for a drawing they will read only once it is finished.

Check every change with a screenshot, saved under a new file name each time, since reading a path you read before can show the earlier image.

## Helpers

The helpers load with the page, so they are back after agent-browser relaunches its browser and you reopen the tab. Each helper takes a shape name and builds the shape id from it with `id(name)`, so one name reaches the same shape through every helper. Each helper that creates a shape runs as one `step`, so the user sees it arrive, and takes an optional `pause`.

The helpers keep the layout with one rule. A shape belongs to the innermost area that holds its top edge. When no area holds it, it belongs to the lowest area of its column whose top edge is above the shape's top edge. An area nested inside another area does not count in that case, so a shape placed under a nested area belongs to the area around it. To place a new shape inside a nested area, pass `into: '<area>'` to the helper that creates the shape. The area grows to hold the shape's top edge before the helper creates the shape. `flow` does the same for a column of shapes. When a shape's height changes, the shapes under it in the same area move by the same amount. The shape's area grows or shrinks to keep a 40-unit margin under the area's lowest shape. An area that sits strictly between another area's left and right edges belongs to that area, even when the inner area starts below the outer area's bottom edge. Growing the outer area does not move the nested area, and the outer area grows to hold the nested area. When an area's height changes, the areas under it in the column move, each with its shapes and the areas nested in it. A nested area that grows moves only the areas under it inside the same outer area; the outer area then grows and moves the areas under it. Place a new shape under the last one in its area, and the helpers grow the area and move the areas under it.

| Helper | What it does |
|---|---|
| `id(name)` | The shape id for a name. |
| `bounds(name)` | The shape's page bounds. |
| `plain(name)` | Reads the shape's text back as plain text, with its line breaks. Use it to edit a text in place instead of keeping a copy of the text in a script. |
| `area(name, { x, y, w, h, label }, pause?)` | Creates an `area` with its label and sends it to the back. With a name that exists, replaces the label, such as a branch's status. |
| `text(name, { x, y, w, text, mono?, size?, into? }, pause?)` | Creates a text of a fixed width, in the hand font or in monospace with `mono: true`. With a name that exists, replaces the text, and moves or widens it when `x`, `y` or `w` are given. With `into`, the named area grows to hold the new shape before the helper creates the shape, so the shape belongs to that area. |
| `card(name, { x, y, w, text, color?, dash?, fill?, mono?, into? }, pause?)` | Creates a rectangle holding a text and fits its height to the text. The rectangle is violet with a semi fill by default. Use it for a question card, a summary box (`color: 'grey', fill: 'solid'`) or a monospace table (`mono: true`). With a name that exists, replaces the text and fits the height to it again. With `into`, the named area grows to hold the new shape before the helper creates the shape, so the shape belongs to that area. |
| `box(name, { x, y, w, h, text, geo?, color?, fill?, dash?, into? }, pause?)` | Creates a diagram node of a fixed size with its text centred. `geo` is `rectangle` (the default), `ellipse` or `cloud`. Use it for the parts of a diagram, coloured by the deployable they belong to. Use `card` for text that sets its own height. With a name that exists, replaces the text. With `into`, the named area grows to hold the new shape before the helper creates the shape, so the shape belongs to that area. |
| `arrow(name, from, to, { text?, bend?, labelPosition?, color?, dash? }, pause?)` | Creates an arrow bound to the centres of the shapes `from` and `to`, so the arrow follows either shape when that shape moves. With a name that exists, changes only the options given. |
| `mermaid(name, { x, y, source }, pause?)` | Creates a `mermaid` shape and sizes it to the diagram's `viewBox`, one canvas unit per diagram unit, once the diagram has rendered. With a name that exists, replaces the source and sizes the shape again. |
| `mock(name, { x, y, w?, kind, data, into? }, pause?)` | Creates a `mock` shape of the given kind with its `data`, 520 units wide unless `w` sets another width, and fits its height to the content. With a name that exists, replaces the `data` and fits the height again. With `into`, the named area grows to hold the new shape first. |
| `note(name, { x, y, w, text }, pause?)` | Creates or updates a Claude note, a grey dashed `card` labelled "Claude". The helper adds the label, so `text` holds only the message. |
| `followUp(name, { summary, note, question? })` | Fills a card with its follow-up under the card's own text: a summary box, a Claude note and, when given, the next question as a card. Replaces the parts of an earlier follow-up. The parts move with the card. |
| `fit(name)` | Zooms to the shape and sets its height from what it holds: a card or a note from its text and its follow-up, a `mermaid` shape from its diagram's `viewBox`, any other `mock` from its `data-root` element scaled from the mockup's natural width, an `area` from its lowest shape. Returns the height, or `null` when the shape isn't drawn. |
| `resize(name, { h?, w? })` | Sets a shape's height or width. A new width on an area widens every top-level area in its column, the areas that share the resized area's left edge. Areas nested inside them keep their width. Each shape to the right of the column moves right by as much as the column area beside it grew, so a shape beside a narrower area clears that area's new edge. A shape beside no column area moves by as much as the resized area grew. |
| `move(name, { x?, y? }, pause?)` | Moves a shape to a new position. A card's follow-up parts move with the card. An area moves with its shapes and its nested areas. The area the shape leaves and the area the shape lands in fit their height again. Move shapes with `move` rather than through `editor.updateShape`, which leaves parts behind and fits no area. |
| `flow(area, names, { top?, gap? })` | Lays the named shapes out one under another inside an area, from `top` (60 units under the area's top edge by default) with `gap` between them (30 by default). The area grows to hold them before they move, so no shape lands past the area's bottom edge, where the next area down would take the shape. |
| `classificationTree(name, spec, { x, y })` | Draws one test branch whole, in one batch, as an `area` labelled `spec.label`: the root as a blue box, each classification as a violet box joined to the root by a line with no arrowheads, each partition as a green box joined the same way, and the matrix under them. A matrix row is its id and summary on the left, a filled dot under each partition it picks, and its expected outcome, kind and setup on the right. A row with `manual: true` is orange. Grey dotted lines run between the rows and down each partition's column, and the dropped rows and the note sit in grey below the matrix. `spec` holds `label`, `root`, `classifications` (each a `name` and its `partitions` as `[key, label]` pairs), `rows` (each `id`, `summary`, `picks` as one partition key per classification, `expected`, `kind`, `setup?` and `manual?`), `dropped?` and `note?`. With a name that exists, draws the branch again in place under fresh ids. |

For example, a question with its follow-up in an open area:

```js
await canvas.card('q4', { x, y, w: 1160, text: '❓ Q4 · <title>\n\n<body>' })
await canvas.followUp('q4', { summary: 'Summary · Q4 so far\n\n<settled and findings>', note: '<how the answer was read>' })
await canvas.note('n2', { text: '<the next reading>' })
```

A session that needs more than these writes its own helpers as scripts in the canvas folder, loads them into the tab, and loads them again after a relaunch.

## Mockups

Mockups import the shared pieces from `@canvas/kit`: `theme`, with the ink, paper, colours, hand font and a sketched border, and `Browser`, a browser window around a screen. Four kinds are built in: `cylinder`, whose data is `{ title, caption }`; `area`, a rounded dashed region whose data is `{ label }`, for grouping the shapes inside a part, used instead of a frame and sent to the back; `mermaid`, whose data is `{ source }`, a mermaid diagram drawn in the canvas's ink and hand font; and `blank-screen`. Use a `mermaid` shape for a finished diagram that will change little. Draw an exploration or an unsettled diagram with tldraw shapes, which are easier to change. A `mermaid` shape scales its diagram to fit and keeps the diagram's proportions. Create it with `mermaid(name, …)`, which sizes it to the diagram. Write and validate the source with superpowers:mermaid. The shape draws with pele, the renderer superpowers:mermaid's PNG comes from, so it looks like that PNG.

Keep them low fidelity: the hand font, sketched borders, and grey bars for text that does not matter.

When the screen has a prototype, copy the mockup from it: the same parts, the same states and the same copy, translated into the language the canvas is written in. A state that is its own view in the prototype is its own mockup on the canvas.

- **Size a mock to its content** when the content's height depends on its data. Give the mockup's root element a `data-root` attribute, and lay it out from the top with no bottom edge. Zoom your tab to the shape, and once the shape has rendered, set the shape's `h` to the root's `offsetHeight` times the shape's width over the mockup's natural width. The canvas renders only the shapes on screen, so a shape measured off screen has no root element. Its `h` then drops to a few units while its content still draws at full size, and every arrow bound to the shape ends at its top edge. `fit(name)` does all of this, and `mock(name, …)` calls it after creating the shape.
- **A shape's `data` holds only JSON.** An `undefined` anywhere inside it fails validation and crashes every open tab; write `null` instead.

## Drawing

- **Notes are free text.** A short sentence with an arrow to the spot it describes. Never a sticky note, since sticky notes are the user's messages.
- **Arrows point at an element's centre**, so they follow when the element moves. An arrow points at a specific spot only when it means that spot: a button, an option, a row.
- **To point at a spot inside a mock**, such as one card in a mockup that draws several, give that element an attribute that names it. Read the element's bounds in the page, convert its corner or edge to a page point with `editor.screenToPage`, and bind the arrow's end to the mock with that point as a `normalizedAnchor`, `isPrecise: true` and `isExact: true`. Without `isExact` the arrow stops at the mock's outer edge.
- Text is black, arrow labels included, and written in tldraw's default font, the hand font (`font: 'draw'`): prose, notes, labels and cards alike. Use the monospace font only where the loading skill asks for it, such as a tree of leaves.
- **Draw each kind of part with its own shape.** Draw each of the system's own modules as a rectangle, coloured by the deployable it belongs to. Draw a store as a cylinder, titled with the product that holds the data, such as `<provider> Postgres`, and captioned with the data it holds. Draw an external service as a cloud, the client as an ellipse, and a platform or a deployable as an `area` around its parts.
- **Label each arrow with the payload or the action it carries**, and with the binding, protocol or credential it goes through when that matters.
- **Spread the canvas across columns instead of letting it grow downwards.** Put related parts in the same column, and start a new column to the right for a part unrelated to the existing ones. Give all top-level areas in a column the same width.
- **Lay a flow out left to right.** Put whoever starts it on the left, stores in a column of their own next to the modules that write them, and external services along the far edge. Draw a process as a vertical column of numbered steps, each with the store or service it reaches on the same row, so its arrow runs straight across.
- **Leave room under a title.** Keep the first shape inside an area clear of the area's label.
- **Keep every shape, label and arrow clear of the others.** When a straight arrow would cross a shape or another arrow's label, curve it with `bend` or move its label with `labelPosition`. When labels crowd each other, move the shapes apart.
- **Leave room for each arrow's label.** Place two shapes joined by a labelled arrow 250 to 300 units apart. With a gap of about 100, the label wraps one word per line over the arrow and the shapes. Keep a label to a few words, since it wraps to the width of its gap. Lay the shapes out with these gaps before drawing the first arrow, instead of fixing collisions after the screenshot.
- **When notes around one diagram would send arrows across it**, centre the diagram and place each note on the side nearest the element it points at, stacked in the same order as their targets so no two arrows cross. When arrows or notes still overlap, add space between the elements or above them and move the notes there.
- **Box the parts of one thing with an `area`, never a frame.** When several separate shapes are parts of the same thing, such as the variants of one part or the screens of one sequence, draw a `mock` shape of kind `area` around them. Send it to the back. Shapes that only sit near each other get no area.
- **Resize an area whenever what it holds grows or moves**, so it keeps a margin around its contents.
- **Set `growY: 0` whenever a script sets a geo shape's `h`.** tldraw keeps the `growY` it computed for the earlier size, and the shape stays taller than what it holds. To stack shapes inside a geo shape under its label, read the label's height first: the height of the shape's `.tl-rich-text` element divided by the zoom level.
- **Delete the arrows of the shapes you delete.** An arrow bound to a deleted shape stays on the canvas where it was drawn. After deleting shapes, delete every arrow with fewer than two bindings.
- **Group what moves together.** Each element, or each set of elements that belong together, is one tldraw group with its title, made with `editor.groupShapes`. Group no further than the smallest set that is one cohesive thing. Elements joined by arrows can share a group, such as the steps of one flow. An element that stands on its own gets its own group, even when an arrow joins it to another element. Arrows between two groups stay outside both, so they stay attached at each end when either group moves.

## Working with the user

- **Your tab holds the current state.** Read what you change from `window.editor` right before changing it, since the user may have moved it. Once the user has edited the canvas, never rebuild it; change only the shapes the change touches.
- **Talking in the chat.** Say what changed and ask in the reply. The user answers in the chat, by voice, or with sticky notes.
- **Talking on the canvas.** Write what you would say in the chat as a Claude note, a grey dashed rectangle labelled `Claude`, in the part of the canvas it is about. The user answers with sticky notes or by voice. The loading skill says which of the two to use; when it does not, ask the user.
- **Never reuse a deleted shape's id.** Sync sends a deleted shape recreated under its id as an update to the old record, so a new shape of another type under that id fails validation in every open tab.
- **A sticky note on the canvas is a message from the user.** When you give the user the URL, tell them to put a sticky note on the shape they want changed, or to draw an arrow from the note to it. `window.canvas.notes()` returns each note with its targets: the shapes an arrow joins it to, else the shapes it sits on, smallest first. Act on each note, and once it is handled, delete it together with its `arrows` and tell the user.
- **"Send to Claude", or Ctrl+. (Cmd+. on a Mac), notifies that a batch of edits is ready.** The document is already saved. While the canvas is open, keep `canvas.sh watch` running under a monitor that notifies you on every line it prints; each line is a click. A background command that reports only when it exits never tells you about a click, and you never read the user's notes. Do not react to the user's edits between clicks. When the monitor expires, start it again.
- **The mic button, or holding Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on a Mac), sends a voice message.** The user holds it while talking and releases it to send; the browser's speech recognition turns the speech into text, in the browser's language unless the URL carries `?lang=<code>`. The watch prints it as `voice: <message>`, followed by ` | selected: <id> (<type>: "<text>"), …` when the user had shapes selected as they released it, and the document is saved first, as with a click. The selected shapes are what the message's "this" or "here" refers to. Treat it as a message from the user in the chat: answer it, and read the canvas for any notes it refers to. A notification can cut a long voice message short. When a message reads as cut off, read its whole line in the watch monitor's output file before acting on it.

## Export

1. **Unslop the texts.** Collect the output of `canvas.sh texts` and the explanatory texts written inside the mockups the document uses into a file in the change's scratch folder, and run superpowers:unslop over it. When that skill is not installed, say so and continue. Apply the findings that survive verification to the canvas and the mockups.
2. **Export.** Run `canvas.sh export`. The loading skill places the SVG where it needs the image.

## Ending

When the loading skill's work is done, or the user moves on to other work, stop the canvas: run `canvas.sh stop` on the document, stop the monitor running `canvas.sh watch`, and close your `agent-browser` tab.

It does not commit.

# Voice flow, enqueue to audio (nagara @ a2a68b1)

Answer: the voice is one free-text string. The client may send it to `POST /items`, and the API stores it in `items.voice` (NOT NULL, no default, no CHECK). The pipeline passes it unchanged to Modal's `/start`. No model name exists anywhere: not in the schema, the API, the pipeline request, the cost ledger or the config. The model is hard-wired to Kokoro in `tts/app.py`. No route lists voices.

## common/ schema
- `common/src/db/schema.ts:50-79` `items` columns: id (`itm`), url, title?, **voice text NOT NULL (:58)**, status (enum + CHECK), created_at, updated_at, queued_at, workflow_instance_id?, current_step?, extraction_domain?, recipe_version_id? (FK), retry_count int default 0, **duration real? (:68), audio_format text? (:69)**, units JSON?, degradations JSON?, error?. Checks: status, units/degradations json_valid.
- Audio-written columns: duration, audio_format, units (timings merged in). There is no TTS model, sample rate or provider column.
- `schema.ts:81-105` `cost_entries`: id (`cst`), item_id FK, type CHECK in (firecrawl, describer, tts), quantity real, unit CHECK in (credits, calls, seconds), dollars real, cached bool default false, detail JSON?, created_at. Index on item_id.
- `common/src/ledger.ts:3-17` defines COST_TYPE/COST_UNIT. The DB has only the initial migration, `common/migrations/0000_initial.sql` (voice at :23, type CHECK at :12).
- `common/src/db/items/create-item.ts:5-8` `createItem(db,{url,voice})` inserts status queued.
- `common/src/db/operations/record-audio.ts:10-24` batch: sets units/duration/audio_format, status ready, and inserts the cost entry.
- `ItemRow = typeof items.$inferSelect` (`common/src/item.ts:12`), so the voice type is `string`.

## api/
- `api/src/routes/enqueue.ts:7-10` valibot body `{url: string, voice?: string}`. Any string is accepted; a wrong shape gives 400 "the body needs a url string and an optional voice string" (:24). `voice: pickVoice(parsed.output.voice)` at :30.
- `api/src/voices.ts:3-17` VOICE_POOL of 10 Kokoro ids (af_heart, af_bella, af_sarah, af_sky, af_aoede, af_alloy, af_nova, am_fenrir, am_michael, am_puck). `pickVoice(voice)` returns `voice ?? random pool entry`. An unknown voice is never validated or rejected; it is stored and fails later in Modal.
- `api/src/response.ts:8-23` `toItemResponse` returns id, url, title, status, voice, created_at, duration and units (only when ready), error, and `audio_url` (`/items/{id}/audio`, only when ready). It returns no model, format or `audio_format`. The response type is inferred; there is no named type in `common/`.
- `api/src/routes/poll.ts` GET item: `requeueIfStale` then `toItemResponse`. `api/src/routes/audio.ts:5-13` 404 unless ready and `audio_format` is set, else a signed redirect to `audioKey(id)`. The format is not used for Content-Type there.
- `api/src/routes/retry.ts:14-58` `claimRetry`, then restart the Workflow. The voice is kept because the row is reused. A retry cannot change the voice.
- Routes (`api/src/index.ts`): enqueue, poll, retry, audio, images, `/health`. No voices-list route.

- `pipeline/src/workflow/steps/synthesis.ts:26-37` `startSynthesisStep` reads the item and sends `{paragraphs: units.map(u=>u.spoken), voice: item.voice, destination: presigned PUT URL}` (:30-34). The destination is a single `audioKey(itemId)`.
- `synthesis.ts:41-52` `waitForSynthesisStep` polls `synthesisResult` every `pollIntervalSeconds`.
- `synthesis.ts:57-85` `storeStep` checks that the timing count equals the unit count (NonRetryable otherwise), then `recordAudio`. The cost entry is `{type:"tts", quantity: duration, unit:"seconds", dollars: duration * env.ttsDollarsPerSecond, detail:{duration}}`. Neither voice nor model is in `detail`.
- `pipeline/src/tts/modal.ts:3-14` types: `SynthesisResult {ready, format "audio/ogg"|"audio/wav", duration, timings[]}` and `SynthesisRequest {paragraphs, voice, destination}`. :22-34 POST `MODAL_START_URL` returns `call_id`. :38-60 GET `MODAL_RESULT_URL?call_id=`: 202 not ready, 410/422 NonRetryable, other non-ok retryable. Auth headers `Modal-Key`/`Modal-Secret` from `MODAL_PROXY_KEY`/`MODAL_PROXY_SECRET` (secrets, `.dev.vars.example:7-8`).
- `pipeline/wrangler.jsonc:40-41` MODAL_START_URL/MODAL_RESULT_URL = `https://asermax--nagara-tts-web.modal.run/{start,result}` (one app, one model); :48 `ttsDollarsPerSecond: 0.000015` (a single global rate). Dev URLs: `pipeline/.dev.vars.example:21-22`. R2_UPLOAD_ENDPOINT/R2_S3_ENDPOINT/R2_BUCKET also feed the upload URL.

## tts/app.py
- :1 docstring "Kokoro-82M on Modal". `StartRequest` (:32-35) `{paragraphs, voice="af_heart", destination}`; the default exists only here.

Base directory for this skill: /home/agus/workspace/asermax/claude-plugins/superpowers/skills/mermaid # Mermaid Diagrams Use a diagram to show something that prose would explain worse: a data model, a flow across services or APIs, a state lifecycle, an object structure. A diagram is worth drawing when the subject has many parts, branches, an order over time or a structure. Do not diagram something one sentence explains. ## How to use this skill 1. Pick the chart type from the chart-selection table below. 2. Open the matching `references/*.md` for that chart's syntax, a worked example and its styling guidance. Load only the references you need. 3. Write the diagram following the common syntax rules. In a flowchart or a state diagram, take each element's shape and colour from the palette in [references/flowchart.md](references/flowchart.md). 4. Validate it, then render it and look at the image (see Validation). Both steps are mandatory. 5. Place the diagram next to the prose it illustrates, not in a separate "diagrams" section. ## Chart selection | You're documenting | Chart | Reference | |---|---|---| | A data model, a schema, database changes (entities, fields, relationships) | `erDiagram` | [references/er-diagram.md](references/er-diagram.md) | | Branching logic, request routing, a flow across a repository's services | `flowchart` | [references/flowchart.md](references/flowchart.md) | | Interaction over time across actors, services or APIs (who calls whom, in what order) | `sequenceDiagram` | [references/sequence-diagram.md](references/sequence-diagram.md) | | The lifecycle or status transitions of an entity | `stateDiagram-v2` | [references/state-diagram.md](references/state-diagram.md) | | Object and type structure and relationships (classes, DTO hierarchies, interfaces) | `classDiagram` | [references/class-diagram.md](references/class-diagram.md) | When two charts fit, such as a flow that could be a `flowchart` or a `sequenceDiagram`, use `sequenceDiagram` when who acts and the order of messages matter, and `flowchart` when branches and decisions matter more than order. ## Common syntax - **Start every diagram with a type declaration**: `flowchart TD`, `sequenceDiagram`, `stateDiagram-v2`, `erDiagram`, `classDiagram`. A block without one does not render. - **Direction** (flowchart and state diagram): `TD` or `TB` runs top-down, `LR` left to right, `BT` bottom-up and `RL` right to left. Use `LR` for pipelines and flows, `TD` for trees and decisions. - **Quote labels with special characters.** Quote any label that contains `()`, `[]`, `{}`, `:`, `,` or quotes: `A["Process (step 1)"]`. Unquoted special characters cause most parse failures. - **Define a node once, then refer to it by id.** Give a node its shape and label on first use (`A[Start]`), then write only `A`. - **Comments** start with `%%` on their own line. - **Leave out decoration and any detail the reader does not need.** ## Validation (mandatory) Diagrams are drawn with [pele](https://pele.run), a renderer that reads mermaid syntax with its own layout engine and visual style. Its syntax is strict, and an invalid diagram renders as an error box instead of a drawing. Validate every diagram before you show it. Write the diagram to a temp file and feed the file to the validator; do not pass a multi-line diagram as an inline shell string, because shell quoting breaks it and the validator reports errors that are not in the diagram. 1. **Write** the raw diagram body (the text between the ` ```mermaid ` fences, without the fences) to a temp file with the `Write` tool, such as `/tmp/diagram.mmd`. 2. **Run** the validator, which reads the diagram from stdin and, given an output path, also renders it to a PNG: ```bash bash /home/agus/workspace/asermax/claude-plugins/superpowers/skills/mermaid/scripts/validate-mermaid.sh /tmp/diagram.png < /tmp/diagram.mmd ``` 3. **Read the result.** The script prints JSON; check `isValid` and `errors[]`: ```json { "isValid": false, "diagramType": "flowchart", "errors": [ { "code": "syntax", "line": 3, "column": 1, "message": "Parse error on line 3: ^ Expecting 'SQE', 'UNICODE_TEXT', 'TEXT', 'TAGSTART', got '$end'" } ] } ``` `code` is one of `syntax`, `semantic`, `unsupported-diagram` and `limit`. Exit codes: `0` valid, `1` invalid, `2` setup error. 4. If the diagram is invalid, **fix** it using the `line` and `message` of each error, then run the validator again until `isValid` is `true`. 5. **Look** at the rendered `/tmp/diagram.png` with the `Read` tool before you show the diagram. A diagram that parses can still draw wrong (see Rendering rules the validator cannot catch). Check for stray nodes or states, overlapping text, and a layout far wider or taller than the page. The script calls pele's own `render()`, so a diagram it accepts is one every pele renderer draws, and the PNG is pele's SVG rasterized with resvg using pele's default light theme. It installs both packages on first run into `~/.cache/claude-plugins/pele/`. Frontmatter and `%%{init}%%` directives are passed to pele, which reads them. ### Fixing common errors - **Unquoted labels with special characters**: wrap them in quotes, `A["Total (USD)"]`, `B{"valid?"}`. - **Wrong arrow for the diagram type**: `-->` in flowcharts, `->>`/`-->>` in sequence diagrams, `-->` in state and class diagrams. Mixing them fails. - **Missing type declaration**: the first line that is not a comment must declare the diagram type. - **`subgraph` or `state` block without its end**: every `subgraph` needs an `end`, and every composite `state X {` needs its `}`. - **A node's shape declared twice**: declare the shape once; later references use the bare id. - **Reserved word as a bare node id**: `end`, `class` and similar ids break parsing; rename the node or quote it. ## Rendering rules the validator cannot catch The parser accepts these, and the renderer draws them wrong. Check for them in the rendered image after validation passes. - **Notes do not wrap.** Pele wraps long text in flowchart nodes, subgraph titles and boxes on its own, but a note in a sequence or state diagram stays on one line and spills past the lifelines or the diagram. Break a long note with `
` at a word boundary. - **A `;` inside state-diagram text ends the statement.** In a note or a transition label, the text after a `;` renders as stray states. Use a comma instead. - **Markdown inside an `@{ shape, label }` label renders as plain text.** Leave markdown out of expanded-shape labels. - **Labels are plain SVG text.** Line breaks, bold and italic render; any other HTML in a label does not. `click` statements that open links work, and JavaScript callbacks are ignored. - **Mermaid themes do not apply.** `theme` and `themeVariables` in an `%%{init}%%` directive change nothing, because pele colours a diagram with CSS variables set by the page it is drawn in. Colours set with `classDef`, `style` and `linkStyle` do apply, and stay fixed when the page switches between light and dark.

"""One short phrase per Phonon en-US female voice (plus Kokoro af_heart), each voice saying its own

from bench import SR, encode_opus

VOICES = ["Zoey", "Juniper", "Everly", "Harper", "Hadley", "Delia"]

tts = ptts.TTS(lang="en")

from kokoro import KPipeline

kokoro = np.concatenate([a for _, _, a in KPipeline(lang_code="a")(PHRASE.format(name="Heart, from Kokoro"), voice="af_heart")])
open("out/voices-short/kokoro-af_heart.ogg", "wb").write(encode_opus(kokoro))

open("out/voices-short/all-phonon-voices.ogg", "wb").write(encode_opus(np.concatenate(clips[:-1])))

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/agus/workspace/asermax/claude-plugins/superpowers/skills/unslop

# Unslop

Edit text to remove AI patterns.

## Process

1. Run a first round: one opus agent, every rule below, the documents in the pass.
2. Verify each finding, then rewrite. Preserve meaning, match intended tone.
3. Run a second round: a fresh agent, the rewritten documents, and the first round's applied report. It checks every applied fix is still in place and flags anything that changed back; verify and re-apply what really slipped, and the pass ends.

## How to scan

The pass is two rounds: the first finds, the second guards what the first fixed.

A fresh agent each round is the point. An agent that has seen its own last report defends the report, repeats what you rejected, and stops looking for what it missed. The second round's agent sees the first round's report on purpose. Its job is not to re-litigate the findings but to verify they survived.

The author cannot run this pass alone, whatever the rules say. Whoever wrote a sentence already decided it earns its place, and that is the judgement the rules ask for.

Agents write nothing. When the text is a draft not yet on disk, save it to a temporary file first so it does not travel through the dispatch message. When the pass covers several documents, one agent takes all of them in the same round, since a sentence that repeats what another document already says is only visible with both open.

### Prompts

The first round:

```
You are doing an editing pass. Read <the file or files>. Do not edit anything.
Do not read anything else.

Apply ONLY the rules below. Read every sentence, and at each one ask what the
reader does differently because of it. Flag the sentence when the answer is
nothing, when it is the answer an earlier sentence already gave, or when it
breaks one of the rules. Report only what one of these rules covers.

RULES:
<every rule under Patterns to detect and fix, verbatim, numbers included>

EXCLUSIONS: an adjectival participle ("the bullets that are missing", "before a
change is done") is not a passive under 29, and an adverb that changes
the truth of the sentence ("skip it silently", "usually already") stays.

OUTPUT: one line per finding, in this format:
<file>:<line> | rule <n> | "<exact quoted span>" | <proposed rewrite>
Only sentences with a finding get a line. End with a line TOTAL: <n>.
Nothing else. No preamble, no summary.
```

The second round:

```
You are verifying an editing pass. Read <the file or files> and the report
below. Do not edit anything. Do not read anything else.

For every finding in the report, check the rewritten text still carries its
fix: the pattern the finding cited is gone and the rewrite kept every fact.
Report only findings whose fix is gone or undone, in this format:
<file>:<line> | rule <n> | "<exact quoted span>"
End with a line TOTAL: <n>. Nothing else. No preamble, no summary.

REPORT:
<the applied findings from the first round, verbatim>
```

### Between rounds

Every line is a claim, not an edit. For each one, reread the span and confirm that it is an instance of the rule cited, that the rewrite keeps every fact and the tone, and that the wording it replaces is not the house form the surrounding documents already use. Drop what fails, apply the rest, then run the second round.

The second round's lines are claims too. Reread each and confirm the fix really is gone or undone before re-applying. When the pass ends, report what both rounds found and what the second round caught slipping back.

## Patterns to detect and fix

Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.

### Content

3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.

### Language

7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
10. **Rule of three.** Don't force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.

### Style

13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example, not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell. A lead-in written as a slogan, a whole claim stated as a motto ("**Shapes say what a thing is.**", "**Nothing overlaps.**"), does not name the item and falls outside that exemption. Make the lead-in the plain instruction itself: "**Draw each kind of part with its own shape.**"
17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
19. **Curly quotes.** Use straight quotes.

### Communication artifacts

20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.

### Filler

23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". Delete "It is important to note that".
24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.

### Jargon

26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate (base), wedge, wedge in (add), vector (way, method), locus, vantage, nexus, primitive as a noun, harness as a metaphor, surface as in "API surface", bedrock, scaffolding as a metaphor, modality, paradigm, gold-plating (more than the job needs), ratchet as a metaphor (the mechanism's real name, or a limit that only tightens), evacuate for moving code (move out), endgame (the last phase), north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. Pick the concrete word.

### Plain speech

27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number, and "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" and "leverage" become "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.
32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), artifacts that talk, figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. "A dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying". Say what you mean. An artifact talks when a shape, label, arrow, name, type or test "says", "shows" or "tells" something to state a rule: "shapes say what a thing is" becomes "draw each module as a rectangle and each store as a cylinder". A sentence that reports what an artifact really produced ("the test shows the bug") stays. Rule 26 covers the metaphor nouns.
33. **Over-compression.** Dropped articles, verbless fragments, symbol-speak, and abbreviations that make the reader decode instead of read. "Parser rejects bad date → exit 2, no write" becomes "The parser rejects a bad date, exits with code 2, and writes nothing." Write whole sentences with their articles and verbs, and spell out arrows and abbreviations.
34. **Describing the message instead of writing it.** Some words refer to the subject. Others refer to the text itself: how many parts it has, what order they come in, that something is about to arrive, that you are about to say it. The second kind carries no information, because the thing being announced arrives in the very next words anyway. Delete it. Then confirm the deletion by checking that every fact survived. These spans sit anywhere in a sentence, not only in front of a colon. At the front: "Two things to take into account:" and "One thing worth doing now:" and "Processing X, the next step is:". Mid-sentence: "the config is fine, but there is one thing worth flagging here". Inside a clause: "I should mention that the build fails on ARM" becomes "the build fails on ARM". Trailing: "which brings us to the next point" just goes. A whole sentence can be this kind too, when its subject is the text or a part of it ("this document", "this section", "the list below") and its verb says what the text is, covers, contains or is for: an opening that states the text's purpose or scope. Delete it, and if a fact appeared only in that sentence, state the fact about the subject instead: "This section explains how the cache expires. Entries expire after an hour." becomes "Cache entries expire after an hour." Same rule for headings: name what is in the section ("Issues found", "Considerations"), do not count it or trail it ("Two things to consider", "What follows"). A count also goes stale the moment an item is added or removed.
35. **Restating what you just said.** A second pass over the same idea, in different words at the same level of detail, telling a reader who understood the first pass nothing new. "That is the thing being deleted" after already naming what to delete. "In other words", "put differently", "that is to say" followed by a paraphrase rather than a sharpening. A closing sentence that recaps the paragraph above it, or an opening sentence and a closing sentence that state the same thesis around a body that already made it. The earlier mention can be anywhere in the text, the title and the description included, so an opening that restates the heading or the description counts too. Ask what the reader can do or know after the second version that they could not after the first. If the answer is nothing, cut it. Keep a restatement only when it adds precision, gives a concrete example, or translates a term the first version assumed the reader knew. A summary that reduces a concept spread over several paragraphs to its main points also stays. 16 is one narrow instance of this, a bold lead that restates its own line.
36. **Pronoun referent overload.** The same pronoun standing for two different things in one sentence, or a relative pronoun dropped where the wrong attachment is the easier parse. "The counts alone do not show a sentence appearing twice, a unit whose text also appears inside the unit before it, or any text it says was left behind": the first "it" is the unit, the second is the tool from the sentence before, and "any text it says was left behind" dropped its "that", so "it says" reads as the verb until "was" breaks the parse. Name the referent, or restore the "that": "inside the previous unit", "any text the tool says was left behind". 28's backtrack test finds the sentence, but splitting cannot repair it: a short sentence can still make the reader resolve one word twice.
37. **Negation where a positive fits.** Double negatives ("not uncommon", "not unlike", "nothing prevents") make the reader invert twice to recover a plain fact, and "not about" framing ("the question is not about X", "this is not a matter of Y") says what something is not while leaving what it is unstated. State the fact: "not uncommon" becomes "common", "not unlike" becomes "like", "the question is not about X" becomes naming what the question is about. A single honest negative stays ("the item does not fail").
38. **Actions turned into nouns.** An event or action written as a noun phrase ("the server failing to start", "the removal of the file", "validation of the input") and then made the subject of a weak verb ("goes in the chat", "happens", "takes place", "is needed"). The reader has to unpack the noun back into who does what to what. Write the clause with its actor and its verb: "Only the server failing to start goes in the chat" becomes "When the server fails to start, tell the user in the chat", and "Validation of the input happens in the parser" becomes "The parser validates the input". A noun stays when it names something the text keeps referring to, such as a defined term ("the migration", "the release").
39. **"What" clauses that withhold the content.** A clause such as "what a thing is", "what flows", "what the arrows cannot show" or "what a system's architecture is" points at information without giving it, and the reader has to guess what belongs there. Replace the clause with the content, or with a concrete example: "label each arrow with what flows" becomes "label each arrow with the payload or action it carries", and "a question about what a system's architecture is" becomes "a question about which parts a system has and how they connect". The clause stays when the words right after it list the content.

# Supporting Kokoro and Phonon with their voices

The settled decisions are in `decisions.md`, numbered in the order the user settled them. The spike's measurements are in `spikes/phonon-vs-kokoro/findings.md`. The canvas `canvas/explore.tldr.json` and its export `canvas/explore.svg` hold the diagrams below with their source notes.

## Today (code at a2a68b1)

An item carries one voice, a free-text string. The client sends it to `POST /items`, or `pickVoice` in `api/src/voices.ts` picks one at random from 10 Kokoro ids. The API stores it in `items.voice` (NOT NULL, no default, no CHECK), the pipeline sends it unchanged in Modal's `/start` request, and every poll returns it. No code outside `tts/` names a model: the Modal app `nagara-tts` hard-codes Kokoro (`KPipeline(lang_code="a")` on an L4), and the pipeline prices every item with one global `ttsDollarsPerSecond`. Nothing validates the voice, so an unknown voice fails inside Modal. Details with file and line references are in `scout-voice-flow.md`, and what the docs commit to is in `docs-voice.md`.

## Proposed data model

| Part | Change | Decisions |
|---|---|---|
| `items.model` | New column, an enum `"kokoro" \| "phonon"` with a CHECK, like `status`. The migration sets `"kokoro"` on existing rows. | 13, 24, 29 |
| `items.voice` | Always a voice of the item's model. | 14, 20 |
| TTS catalog in `common/` | New. Each model's voices and default voice, and the default model. Kokoro: its American voices (`af_*`, `am_*`), default `af_heart`. Phonon: its 12 American voices, default `Zoey`. Default model: Kokoro. | 18, 23, 25, 27, 28 |
| Enqueue body | Gains `model?`. The API applies the default model, then the model's default voice, and answers 400 when the voice does not belong to the model. No random pick. | 15, 16, 20 |
| `VOICE_POOL` and `pickVoice` | Removed. | 20 |
| Item response | Carries `model` next to `voice`, on `GET /items/:id` and on the enqueue response, which uses the same `toItemResponse`. | 22 |
| Modal `/start` request | Gains `model`. One app spawns the matching class: Kokoro on an L4, Phonon on 1 CPU core with `ptts==0.4.1`, both with `scaledown_window=300` and a snapshot. One `MODAL_START_URL` stays. | 12, 26, 30, 31 |
| Cost row | Same shape. `dollars` = audio seconds × the model's rate, with the rates in the pipeline's config: Kokoro about 0.0000084 and Phonon about 0.0000028 dollars per audio second (warm compute only). | 17, 21 |

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant A as API Worker
    participant D as D1
    participant P as Pipeline Worker
    participant M as Modal TTS
    C->>A: POST /items {url, model?, voice?}
    A->>A: model = model or default model
    A->>A: voice = voice or the model's default voice
    alt voice not in the model's voices
        A-->>C: 400
    else voice matches the model
        A->>D: insert item (model, voice)
        A-->>C: item
    end
    P->>D: read item.model, item.voice
    P->>M: /start {paragraphs, model, voice, destination}
    M-->>P: format, duration, timings
    P->>D: audio fields + tts cost (duration x rate of model)
    C->>A: GET /items/:id
    A-->>C: model?, voice, audio_url
```

## Code the change touches

- `common/src/db/schema.ts` and a generated migration for `items.model` (invariant 7); `createItem` and `ItemRow` gain the model.
- `api/src/routes/enqueue.ts`: the valibot body, the defaults and the voice check. `api/src/voices.ts` gives way to the catalog.
- `pipeline/src/workflow/steps/synthesis.ts` and `pipeline/src/tts/modal.ts`: the start request carries the model, and the store step prices with the model's rate. `pipeline/wrangler.jsonc` holds one rate per model.
- `tts/app.py`: a Phonon class next to Kokoro, `StartRequest` gains the model, and the `af_heart` default moves out.
- Tests: about 7 fixtures with `af_heart`, `api/test/enqueue.test.ts` (it duplicates `VOICE_POOL` and requests `bf_emma`, which decisions 14, 16 and 18 now reject), and the Modal fake in `pipeline/test/helpers/services.ts`.
- Docs (decision 19): `product-design/queue.md` ("Voices"), `technical-design/item-contract.md`, `item-lifecycle.md`, `tts-service.md`, `persistence-and-storage.md` and `product-design/what-nagara-is.md`.

## Not verified

- Whether redeploying the Modal app after a change to one class discards the other class's snapshot (decision 26 skipped the spike that would tell).
- The spike's full-article timings and Whisper check used the Phonon voice Hadley, not the default Zoey.

Turns a session's friction into something reusable. The plugin grows this way, by keeping the corrections the user just made by hand instead of designing a pipeline upfront.

## Modes

Pick the mode from what the user asks.

- **Discovery.** Follow `references/discover.md` when the user asks for nothing specific, or asks what the session, or a part of it, has to teach.
- **Directed.** Follow `references/directed.md` when the user names what to build.
- **Mixed.** When the user names some items and also asks what else there is, work the named items as directed and run discovery over the part of the session the ask points at.

Before starting, tell the user which mode you are following. For a mixed ask, list the items you work as directed and the part of the session discovery covers. Every mode continues with Drafting once there is an item to draft.

## Fidelity

Anything produced here reproduces the patterns the session established exactly. The formats, the visualizations, the wording of a rule, the order of steps, and every correction the user made along the way are the specification. Do not adapt them, improve them, or generalize them into something the session did not do.

Examples inside a skill or wiki entry are generic. They carry the shape the session used, with placeholders in place of the session's tickets, repositories and field names. A code example in a wiki entry names its components, hooks, endpoints and fields after a generic resource, such as `ResourceActionButton` or `useResourceAction`, never after the session's feature.

## Drafting

1. **Classify and scope each item before drafting it.** Process becomes a skill, new or iterated. Work a skill should hand to a subagent becomes an agent. Knowledge about a tool or technology becomes a wiki entry. A decision the user repeated for this project becomes a standing rule in a local file. A rule every change to this project respects, about how the product behaves or how the system is built, becomes a line in the project's invariants note. Global means useful in any project; local means true only for this one. Restate the job the item does, which kind it is and where it lands. Read the skill, entry or index it would land in to check it is not already there; if it already says this, the finding becomes an iteration on whatever failed to read it. Draft only once the user confirms the shape.

2. **Draft every item in one reply**, ordered by confidence then by impact, each under its own heading, with the file it lands in. For a new skill, agent, wiki entry, design type or program design representation, give the full text; for an iteration, the old and new text. Before showing the drafts, write them to the change's scratch folder, per the convention in mahou:basics, and run `superpowers:unslop` over them. The user approves, corrects or drops each item separately; do not ask for a single approve-everything answer, though the user may give one.

   - A new skill: the full draft, following the new skill checklist.
   - A skill iteration: the exact change and the reason it is needed.
   - An agent: the full draft, plus the change to the skill that dispatches it.
   - A wiki entry: the draft plus its line in the index at the right level.
   - A local file: the draft and which skill it changes.

3. **Write each approved item** to its place. Leave everything uncommitted.

## Where things land

| Finding | Lands as |
|---|---|
| Reusable process | `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` in the plugin |
| Work a skill should hand to a subagent | `agents/<name>.md` in the plugin, dispatched by the skill that needs it |
| Knowledge about a tool or technology | `skills/wiki/references/<topic>/<entry>.md`, plus its line in that folder's `INDEX.md` |
| A design type that generalizes beyond the session it came from | `skills/design/references/types/<type>.md`, plus its row in the types table of mahou:design. A type specific to one change stays out |
| A program design representation that generalizes beyond the session it came from | `skills/program-design/references/representations/<form>.md`, plus its row in the representations table of mahou:program-design. A form specific to one change stays out |
| A rule or fact true only for this project | `.mahou/<skill>.md`, or `.mahou/wiki/` with the same index-per-level shape as the global store |
| A rule every change to this project respects | A line in the project's invariants note, in the section for its kind, linking the note that explains it when one does |

## New skill checklist

- A descriptive name. The magic vocabulary stays in mahou:basics and the README.
- One job. Two jobs means proposing two skills.
- A description precise enough to load when intended, and to let mahou:guide match goals to it. Descriptions that overlap an existing skill's are the main way routing degrades.
- First lines of the body: load mahou:basics, then read `.mahou/<skill>.md` if present.
- No decisions delegated to the agent. It maps the state and asks; the user settles. A draft that contains "choose the best option" or "decide whether" is not ready.
- Nothing committed as a side effect.

## Removing or replacing a skill

When an item replaces an existing skill, the replacement is not done until the old directory is removed and every reference to it is updated: the plugin README and every skill that names it. List those edits as part of the item.

## Committing

Propose, never commit. When the user accepts an item, write the files and stop. Version bumps belong to whatever commits the marketplace; never hand-edit a `plugin.json` version.

I'm running **discovery mode** over the whole session. These are the points where the flow changed course, in the order they happened.

**1. Building `ptts` with CUDA failed twice before it worked.** In spike round 2 the Modal image build failed against CUDA 12.4: `xn` 0.2.11 uses cuBLASLt enums that only CUDA 12.8 has. With 12.8 the build failed again, because maturin wanted `patchelf` to bundle the CUDA libraries into the wheel. `--auditwheel skip` got past it. I had to find both facts by trial. The `modal` wiki folder only covers web endpoints, so neither fact is written anywhere.

**2. The Cloudflare Container spike hit platform behaviour I hadn't expected.**
- The Worker answered 403 to Python's default `urllib` user agent.
- The first call after a deploy, and one later cold call, returned 500.
- Neither `container.stop()` nor `sleepAfter = "30s"` reliably stopped the instance, so I couldn't measure cold starts on demand.
- `wrangler containers instances` takes the application ID, not its name.

The global `cloudflare/containers` entry covers sizes, sleep and cost. I didn't read it during the spike, because the basics rule says to read entries only when asked. A grep of it shows none of these four facts.

**3. You had to ask whether the Kokoro L4 numbers were cold or cached.** My report compared all setups warm, but never said so, and it left the cold numbers out. That gap is what led to round 4. The mahou:report skill and the spike findings format don't ask a measurement to state its conditions (cold or warm, snapshot or not).

**4. I told you Phonon's memory snapshot "apparently was never used". That reading was wrong.** When you asked why, Modal's logs showed each cold call had created a snapshot: CPU functions need about 6 before restores start. I had concluded it from load times without reading the platform's logs first. No wiki entry covers Modal memory snapshots: how many cold starts a CPU function needs before it restores, the log lines that tell creating from restoring, and `modal app logs <id> --since` working on a stopped app.

**5. You asked for the price comparison while the core-count round was running.** The round measured speed only. You added "include pricing comparison with kokoro" mid-turn. Earlier rounds had included cost, so the format was in session memory, not in the spike's instructions.

**6. You wanted short voice samples, and to open them yourself.** I had produced one paragraph per voice. You asked for "una frase muy cortita" per voice. Each voice then said its own name in one file, and you asked me to `xdg-open` the folder. The canvas had no way to play audio, and local `spike.md` only says browser audio plays muted. Listening went around the canvas.

**7. My first canvas diagram drew the whole process when you wanted the data model and a simple sequence.** You asked to "diagram the existing design for how we manage the items and its voices". I drew the full architecture flow across Workers, Modal and R2, following explore-with-canvas and architecture-exploration's layout rules. You said "hubo una confusión… no era el proceso entero sino más bien el modelado y quizás un diagrama de secuencia más sencillo". Neither skill says how to choose between a data model, a sequence and an architecture drawing when the user asks for "the design".

**8. Canvas cards overlapped and you pointed at it ("se sobreescribieron acá algunas cosas").** Twice, after a `move` or a follow-up on a question card nested inside another card's follow-up, the nested card's follow-up parts landed on top of other text. A `followUp` without a `note` also rendered the text "undefined". I fixed it by redrawing follow-ups in place. These look like defects in the canvas helpers (`move`, `followUp`), not in the skill text.

**9. Some answers to two-option questions were ambiguous.** You answered "exactamente" to an A-or-B card, and "No la cerremos" to the Cloudflare card, where speech recognition could have meant either option. Both needed another round. My question cards often offered two options inside one question, which invites a yes/no answer. The design-tree and explore question rules don't say how to phrase a card when the answer will come by voice.

**10. You asked for a review of contradictions and open items.** "¿algo más que tengamos que explorar, alguna contradicción en las decisiones o algo pendiente?" Explore has no step that rereads the settled set for conflicts with each other, with the docs, or with the tests. I improvised the Review area.

**11. You asked for a written summary in the scratch folder at the end.** Explore says "write no report; the conversation is the record". Basics only requires decisions to be in a file. You asked to put "todo lo relevante" into the scratch folder before closing, so I wrote `exploration.md` with today's design, the proposed design and the code it touches.

Do these match what you remember? Anything to add, drop or correct before you pick what to keep?
